claim: Following the retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheet 10–20 k years ago, the parallel evolution of freshwater ecotypes from ancestral marine forms has occurred repeatedly and independently in thousands of populations across the Northern Hemisphere.
source: Following the retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheet 10–20 k years ago, the parallel evolution of freshwater ecotypes from ancestral marine forms has occurred repeatedly and independently in thousands of populations across the Northern Hemisphere (Bell and Foster, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bell and Foster, 1994

claim: Forward mapping and functional dissection have identified mutations in cis-regulatory elements underlying the parallel loss of bony armor plates in sticklebacks.
source: Firstly, forward mapping and functional dissection have identified mutations in cis-regulatory elements underlying the parallel loss of major morphological traits (bony armor plates Colosimo et al., 2005; O'Brown et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Colosimo et al., 2005 and O'Brown et al., 2015

claim: Forward mapping and functional dissection have identified mutations in cis-regulatory elements underlying the parallel loss of pelvic spines in sticklebacks.
source: Firstly, forward mapping and functional dissection have identified mutations in cis-regulatory elements underlying the parallel loss of major morphological traits (bony armor plates Colosimo et al., 2005; O'Brown et al., 2015) and pelvic spines Shapiro et al., 2004; Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shapiro et al., 2004 and Chan et al., 2010

claim: Whole genome sequencing of marine and freshwater sticklebacks from multiple populations revealed that repeated parallel evolution of freshwater ecotypes from marine ancestors involves reuse of pre-existing genetic variation at ~81 loci across the genome.
source: Further, whole genome sequencing of marine and freshwater sticklebacks from multiple populations revealed that repeated parallel evolution of freshwater ecotypes from marine ancestors involves reuse of pre-existing genetic variation at ~81 loci across the genome that are repeatedly involved in parallel evolution (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones et al., 2012

claim: The loci repeatedly involved in parallel evolution in sticklebacks are predominantly intergenic and thus may act through regulatory mechanisms.
source: These loci are predominantly intergenic and thus may act through regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that loci are intergenic

claim: Expression changes in osmoregulatory genes has been linked to freshwater adaptation by anadromous ancestors in sticklebacks and other fish.
source: Expression changes in osmoregulatory genes has been linked to freshwater adaptation by anadromous ancestors in sticklebacks and other fish (Gibbons et al., 2017; Velotta et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gibbons et al., 2017 and Velotta et al., 2017

claim: Freshwater adaptation in sticklebacks and other fish is associated with changes in gene expression plasticity.
source: Further, previous studies have shown that freshwater adaptation in sticklebacks and other fish is associated with changes in gene expression plasticity (Gunter et al., 2017; McCairns and Bernatchez, 2010; Whitehead, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gunter et al., 2017, McCairns and Bernatchez, 2010, and Whitehead, 2010

claim: The stickleback gill transcriptome contains 29295 transcribed loci, 17304 of which are multi-transcript loci with 171620 different transcripts combined.
source: The stickleback gill transcriptome contains 29295 transcribed loci, 17304 of which are multi-transcript loci with 171620 different transcripts combined.
evidence: Based on data from reference-guided transcriptome assembly

claim: The stickleback gill transcriptome contains considerably more transcripts than Ensembl gene build 90 for the stickleback genome.
source: This is considerably more than Ensembl gene build 90 for the stickleback genome (22456 loci, 29245 transcripts), likely because of the higher sequencing coverage of the current dataset compared to the low coverage EST libraries used to inform gene annotations of Ensembl's genebuild (Kingsley et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on comparison to Ensembl gene build 90 and citation to Kingsley et al., 2004

claim: The transcriptome includes 7147 novel transcribed loci that do not overlap with any transcript in Ensembl gene build v90.
source: The transcriptome includes 7147 novel transcribed loci that do not overlap with any transcript in Ensembl gene build v90.
evidence: Based on comparison of assembled transcriptome to Ensembl gene build v90

claim: Candidate coding regions with complete open-reading frames and likelihood scores > 20 were identified for 1018 novel loci using TransDecoder.
source: Of these novel loci, candidate coding regions with complete open-reading frames and likelihood scores > 20 were identified for 1018 using TransDecoder (Haas et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on data from TransDecoder analysis and citation to Haas et al., 2013

claim: At the locus level the assembly shows very high sensitivity (Sn = 81%) with few false negatives (fSn = 100%) and moderate specificity (Sp = 59%, fSp = 69%).
source: At the locus level our assembly shows very high sensitivity (Sn = 81%) with few false negatives (fSn = 100%) and moderate specificity reflective of the appreciable number of novel coding regions we detected relative to the Ensembl gene build 90 (Sp = 59%, fSp = 69%).
evidence: Based on comparison of assembly to Ensembl gene build 90

claim: 21399 (73%) of loci were expressed at FPKM >= 1 in at least one of the 20 marine and freshwater fish analyzed.
source: Considering the raw FPKM data 21399 (73%) of loci were expressed at FPKM >= 1 in at least one of the 20 marine and freshwater fish analyzed, and 16195 (55%) in more than 10 individuals.
evidence: Based on FPKM expression data from RNA-seq

claim: 16195 (55%) of loci were expressed in more than 10 individuals.
source: Considering the raw FPKM data 21399 (73%) of loci were expressed at FPKM >= 1 in at least one of the 20 marine and freshwater fish analyzed, and 16195 (55%) in more than 10 individuals.
evidence: Based on FPKM expression data from RNA-seq

claim: The most highly expressed group of genes shows strong enrichment for biological processes with the respiratory function of the gill including mitochondrial respiration, ATP synthesis coupled proton transport and cytoplasmic translation.
source: Hierarchical clustering of expression levels revealed that the gill transcriptome can be characterized by five major groups of loci based on their average expression level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) with the most highly expressed group of genes showing strong enrichment for biological processes with the respiratory function of the gill including mitochondrial respiration, ATP synthesis coupled proton transport and cytoplasmic translation (Appendix 1).
evidence: Based on hierarchical clustering analysis and gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Appendix 1

claim: Principal components 2 and 5 are major axes of variation (14.5% and 6.3% PVE, respectively) that separate marine and freshwater transcriptomes.
source: While the first major axis of variation separates individuals by river system (24% variation explained, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), we identified PC2 and PC5 as major axes of variation (14.5% and 6.3% PVE, respectively, Figure 1c) that separate marine and freshwater transcriptomes.
evidence: Based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Parallel transcriptome divergence is highly correlated with river-specific measures of marine-freshwater transcriptome divergence.
source: Parallel transcriptome divergence is highly correlated with river-specific measures of marine-freshwater transcriptome divergence (log of marine/freshwater expression fold change in the River Tyne and Little Campbell Rivers, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Parallel divergence of gene expression between marine and freshwater ecotypes reared under common environmental conditions represents only a small proportion of transcriptome variation.
source: Similar to the only 0.01% parallel genetic divergence observed at the genomic DNA level (Jones et al., 2012), here parallel divergence of gene expression between marine and freshwater ecotypes reared under common environmental conditions represents only a small proportion of transcriptome variation.
evidence: Based on comparison to genomic DNA divergence from Jones et al., 2012 and PCA analysis

claim: 586 transcripts show the highest contribution toward parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence (top or bottom 1% composite PC loadings, median FDR over outliers 2.6%).
source: From here on we refer to loci with the highest contribution toward parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence (top or bottom 1% composite PC loadings, median FDR over outliers 2.6%, N = 586 transcripts, Figure 1—figure supplement 5) as 'parallel diverged loci'.
evidence: Based on composite PC analysis and FDR calculation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: The parallel diverged loci show an enrichment in gene ontology processes and molecular functions associated with gill ion exchange, osmoregulation and blood traits.
source: The parallel diverged loci show an enrichment in gene ontology processes and molecular functions associated with gill ion exchange, osmoregulation and blood traits (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Supplementary file 3

claim: Top ranking genes with parallel expression divergence include Na-Cl cotransporter (slc12a10), Basolateral Na-K-Cl Symporter (slc12a2), cation proton antiporter 3 (slc9a3.2), Potassium Inwardly-Rectifying Voltage-Gated Channel (kcnj1a.3), potassium voltage-gated channel (KCNA2), Epithelial Calcium Channel 2 (trpv6), Sodium/Potassium-Transporting ATPase (atp1a1.4), aquaporin 3a (aqp3a), and carbonic anhydrase 2 (ca2).
source: Top ranking genes include Na-Cl cotransporter (slc12a10), Basolateral Na-K-Cl Symporter (slc12a2), cation proton antiporter 3 (slc9a3.2), Potassium Inwardly-Rectifying Voltage-Gated Channel (kcnj1a.3), potassium voltage-gated channel (KCNA2), Epithelial Calcium Channel 2 (trpv6), Sodium/Potassium-Transporting ATPase (atp1a1.4), aquaporin 3a (aqp3a), and carbonic anhydrase 2 (ca2) — genes known to play a role in osmoregulation in fish and other organisms.
evidence: Based on gene ontology enrichment analysis and established knowledge about osmoregulation genes

claim: Transcripts with parallel expression divergence are distributed across all 21 chromosomes.
source: Transcripts with parallel expression divergence are distributed across all 21 chromosomes (Figure 2a)
evidence: Based on genomic distribution shown in Figure 2a

claim: Transcripts with parallel expression divergence are more proximal to genomic regions undergoing parallel marine-freshwater adaptive divergence at the DNA sequence level than expected by chance.
source: Transcripts with parallel expression divergence are distributed across all 21 chromosomes (Figure 2a), and more proximal to genomic regions undergoing parallel marine-freshwater adaptive divergence at the DNA sequence level than expected by chance (identified in Jones et al., 2012), randomization test, p<<0.025; Figure 2b–c).
evidence: Based on randomization test and proximity analysis shown in Figure 2b-c, with reference to adaptive loci from Jones et al., 2012

claim: More than 13% of transcripts with parallel expression divergence were found within 10 kb of regions of parallel genetic divergence.
source: More than 13% of transcripts with parallel expression divergence were found within 10 kb of regions of parallel genetic divergence; and nearly 40% within 75 kb (Figure 2c)
evidence: Based on proximity analysis shown in Figure 2c

claim: Nearly 40% of transcripts with parallel expression divergence were found within 75 kb of regions of parallel genetic divergence.
source: More than 13% of transcripts with parallel expression divergence were found within 10 kb of regions of parallel genetic divergence; and nearly 40% within 75 kb (Figure 2c)
evidence: Based on proximity analysis shown in Figure 2c

claim: In Little Campbell fish, loci with parallel expression divergence show a reduction in nucleotide diversity (Pi) within each ecotype around the transcription start sites.
source: In Little Campbell fish, we observed a reduction in nucleotide diversity (Pi) within each ecotype around the TSSs of transcripts with parallel expression divergence (Figure 2f–g).
evidence: Based on nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 2f-g

claim: In Little Campbell fish, reduced within-population diversity around transcription start sites of parallel diverged transcripts was accompanied by increased genetic divergence (FST) centered on TSSs with a slight upstream bias.
source: Reduced within-population diversity was accompanied by increased genetic divergence (FST) that was centered on TSSs with a slight upstream bias (Figure 2e).
evidence: Based on FST analysis shown in Figure 2e

claim: In River Tyne, a slightly increased FST was observed around the TSSs of transcripts with parallel expression divergence, but no reduction in nucleotide diversity relative to other transcripts was detected.
source: In contrast, although we observed a slightly increased FST around the TSSs of transcripts with parallel expression divergence in the River Tyne, we did not detect a reduction in nucleotide diversity relative to other transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), possibly due to concurrent selective sweeps on different haplotype backgrounds (also referred to as soft sweeps) in this younger population.
evidence: Based on FST and nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: 3807 (13%), 4472 (15%), 7716 (26%) and 10102 (34.5%) non-sex-biased genes could be assayed for cis- vs trans-mediated expression in at least one F1 individual from Tyne, Shiel, Forss and Little Campbell, respectively.
source: Considering all expressed loci in the gill, 3807 (13%), 4472 (15%), 7716 (26%) and 10102 (34.5%) non-sex-biased genes could be assayed for cis- vs trans-mediated expression in at least one F1 individual from Tyne, Shiel, Forss and Little Campbell, respectively.
evidence: Based on allele-specific expression analysis of F1 hybrids

claim: In each ecotype-pair, marine-freshwater expression differences are predominantly driven by divergence in cis-regulation.
source: In each ecotype-pair, marine-freshwater expression differences are predominantly driven by divergence in cis-regulation (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Based on allele-specific expression analysis shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The degree of cis-divergence scales positively with the degree of genetic divergence between marine and freshwater ecotypes from each river system.
source: In each ecotype-pair, marine-freshwater expression differences are predominantly driven by divergence in cis-regulation (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), with the degree of cis-divergence scaling positively with the degree of genetic divergence (measured either as the number of fixed differences or mean per site nucleotide divergence between the parents) between marine and freshwater ecotypes from each river system.
evidence: Based on correlation between cis-divergence and genetic divergence shown in Figure 3b

claim: From ~350 to ~2000 transcripts were classified as cis-diverged across the four river systems.
source: Across the four river systems, from ~350 to ~2000 transcripts were classified as cis-diverged (with Little Campbell River fish showing the highest number,~2000, or ~20%, of cis- divergence. See also Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on classification of regulatory divergence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Little Campbell River fish showed the highest number of cis-diverged transcripts (~2000, or ~20%).
source: Across the four river systems, from ~350 to ~2000 transcripts were classified as cis-diverged (with Little Campbell River fish showing the highest number,~2000, or ~20%, of cis- divergence. See also Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on classification of regulatory divergence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: 181 and 68 parallel diverged loci were testable for allele-specific analysis in Little Campbell and Tyne, respectively.
source: After filtering, 181 and 68 parallel diverged loci were testable in Little Campbell and Tyne, respectively.
evidence: Based on filtering of parallel diverged loci for allele-specific analysis

claim: Loci with parallel divergence in expression showed a significant excess of cis-regulation (16–26% and 11–12% above average in Tyne and Little Campbell F1 offspring respectively) compared to random expectations.
source: Loci with parallel divergence in expression showed a significant excess of cis-regulation (16–26% and 11–12% above average in Tyne and Little Campbell F1 offspring respectively) and cis+trans regulation (above average), compared to random expectations obtained by 1000 random draws of equal size from all genes that showed expression divergence between ecotypes (see Materials and methods) (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on randomization test shown in Figure 4

claim: Loci with parallel divergence in expression showed a significant excess of cis+trans regulation compared to random expectations.
source: Loci with parallel divergence in expression showed a significant excess of cis-regulation (16–26% and 11–12% above average in Tyne and Little Campbell F1 offspring respectively) and cis+trans regulation (above average), compared to random expectations obtained by 1000 random draws of equal size from all genes that showed expression divergence between ecotypes (see Materials and methods) (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on randomization test shown in Figure 4

claim: The overrepresentation of trans-acting divergence in parallel diverged loci was lower (between 6–16% and 0–2% in Tyne and Little Campbell, respectively) and not different from random expectation in all F1s.
source: In contrast, the overrepresentation of trans-acting divergence was lower, between 6–16% and 0–2%, respectively, and not different from random expectation in all F1s.
evidence: Based on randomization test comparing to random expectations

claim: Parallel diverging transcripts from both rivers showed a significant excess of cis- and trans-regulation of expression divergence acting in the same direction (divergence in cis+trans co-regulation).
source: In parallel diverging transcripts, ecotype-pairs from both rivers further showed a significant excess of cis- and trans-regulation of expression divergence acting in the same direction (divergence in cis+trans co-regulation).
evidence: Based on analysis of regulatory divergence patterns

claim: The observed excess of cis+trans regulation in transcripts that contribute to parallel expression divergence is consistent with directional selection, as opposed to genetic drift.
source: The observed excess of cis+trans regulation in the transcripts that contribute to parallel expression divergence, is consistent with directional selection, as opposed to genetic drift, which should influence amplifying (cis+trans) and canceling (cis-trans) divergence equally (Fraser et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on inference from theory and citation to Fraser et al., 2010

claim: The candidate genes slc12a2, atp1a1.2, trpv6 and aqp3a that are involved in teleost ion homeostasis were among the parallel diverged transcripts influenced by cis+trans acting regulatory divergence.
source: Notably, the candidate genes slc12a2, atp1a1.2, trpv6 and aqp3a that are involved in teleost ion homeostasis were among the parallel diverged transcripts influenced by cis+trans acting regulatory divergence.
evidence: Based on identification of specific genes with cis+trans regulation and established knowledge about their function

claim: Parallel divergent loci that are upregulated in freshwater show strong positive correlations among populations in their quantitative extent of both cis- and trans-divergence.
source: Parallel divergent loci that are upregulated in freshwater show strong positive correlations among populations in their quantitative extent of both cis- and trans-divergence (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The correlation in cis- and trans-divergence is lost in loci that do not contribute to parallel expression divergence (composite PC loadings close to zero).
source: This correlation is lost in loci that do not contribute to parallel expression divergence (composite PC loadings close to zero) and is less consistent among parallel divergent loci downregulated in freshwater fish.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis across different subsets of loci

claim: The correlation in cis- and trans-divergence is less consistent among parallel divergent loci downregulated in freshwater fish.
source: This correlation is lost in loci that do not contribute to parallel expression divergence (composite PC loadings close to zero) and is less consistent among parallel divergent loci downregulated in freshwater fish.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis across different subsets of loci

claim: Divergently expressed genes upregulated in freshwater fish show greater effect size in both cis- and trans- components than their freshwater downregulated counterparts.
source: Again, we found that the magnitude of cis- and trans-divergence is not symmetrical: divergently expressed genes upregulated in freshwater fish show greater effect size in both cis- and trans- components than their freshwater downregulated counterparts (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of effect sizes shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Cis-regulatory divergence showed the strongest level of additivity among all regulatory classes.
source: Taking into account all four F1-parent comparisons, cis-regulatory divergence showed the strongest level of additivity (Figure 6a)
evidence: Based on dominance-additivity ratio analysis shown in Figure 6a

claim: Cis-regulatory divergence is linked to higher additivity of between-species expression differences.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that cis-divergence is linked to higher additivity of between-species expression differences (Lemos et al., 2008; McManus et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lemos et al., 2008 and McManus et al., 2010

claim: Cis-regulatory divergence tended to be most stable across genetic backgrounds indicating that cis-acting divergence is least influenced by epistasis.
source: Our results, consistent in both Tyne and Little Campbell crosses, show that cis-regulatory divergence tends to be most stable across genetic backgrounds (Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) making it a favorable substrate for adaptive divergence.
evidence: Based on analysis of regulatory divergence sharing between siblings shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: A total of 2542 transcripts were differentially expressed between at least two salinity treatments (FDR 1%).
source: A total of 2542 transcripts were differentially expressed between at least two salinity treatments (FDR 1%), consistent with major changes in gill structure and function upon salinity acclimation (Hwang et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on differential expression analysis and citation to Hwang et al., 2011

claim: Differences between salinity treatments were mostly driven by freshwater acclimation (0.2 ppt), which elicited a response markedly different from both standard husbandry conditions (3.5 ppt) and typical marine salinity (35 ppt).
source: Differences between salinity treatments were mostly driven by freshwater acclimation (0.2 ppt), which elicited a response markedly different from both standard husbandry conditions (3.5 ppt) and typical marine salinity (35 ppt) (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on analysis of salinity response shown in Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: An unexpectedly high proportion of parallel diverged transcripts (97 of 586) showed an effect of salinity on expression level (hypergeometric test p<4.3e-6).
source: We observed that an unexpectedly high proportion of parallel diverged transcripts also showed an effect of salinity on expression level (97 of 586, hypergeometric test p<4.3e-6), suggesting a large proportion of the parallel diverged transcripts in the gill are involved in physiological responses to water salinity.
evidence: Based on hypergeometric test of overlap between parallel diverged transcripts and salinity-responsive transcripts

claim: Despite the observed plastic response of gene expression to salinity, the degree of cis-divergence of salinity-responsive genes with parallel expression divergence was highly correlated across salinities.
source: Despite the observed plastic response of gene expression (Figure 6c, left triangle), the degree of cis-divergence of salinity-responsive genes with parallel expression divergence was highly correlated across salinities (Figure 6c, right triangle), indicating that the observed salinity response was not caused by cis-regulatory divergence but largely due to trans-acting regulation that influenced the expression of both alleles in similar magnitude.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of allele-specific expression across salinities shown in Figure 6c

claim: The observed salinity response was not caused by cis-regulatory divergence but largely due to trans-acting regulation that influenced the expression of both alleles in similar magnitude.
source: Despite the observed plastic response of gene expression (Figure 6c, left triangle), the degree of cis-divergence of salinity-responsive genes with parallel expression divergence was highly correlated across salinities (Figure 6c, right triangle), indicating that the observed salinity response was not caused by cis-regulatory divergence but largely due to trans-acting regulation that influenced the expression of both alleles in similar magnitude.
evidence: Based on inference from correlation analysis of allele-specific expression shown in Figure 6c

claim: Cis-regulatory changes provide a mechanism for genetic assimilation of plastic responses into heritable variation where the effects of regulatory alleles are independent of the environment.
source: Based on these results we hypothesize that cis-regulatory changes provide a mechanism for genetic assimilation of plastic responses into heritable variation (Waddington, 1942) where the effects of regulatory alleles are independent of the environment.
evidence: Based on hypothesis derived from salinity experiment results and citation to Waddington, 1942

claim: Parallel transcriptomic divergence involves only a few hundred genes each with relatively small effect on expression divergence.
source: We found that when sticklebacks are reared under the same standard husbandry conditions, parallel transcriptomic divergence involves only a few hundred genes each with relatively small effect on expression divergence, similar to the small proportion of the genome that shows parallel adaptive divergence at the DNA sequence level (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on PCA analysis and comparison to genomic divergence from Jones et al., 2012

claim: Parallel divergently expressed genes are proximal to adaptive loci identified from signatures of parallel divergence at the sequence level.
source: Parallel divergently expressed genes are proximal to adaptive loci identified from signatures of parallel divergence at the sequence level, and support a role for the reuse of ancient standing genetic variation in the parallel adaptive divergence of gene expression.
evidence: Based on proximity analysis and inference about standing genetic variation

claim: A large proportion of loci with marine-freshwater divergent expression was unique to a local river system.
source: We also observed a large proportion of loci with marine-freshwater divergent expression that was unique to a local river system (see Appendix 1) indicating there is room for drift and/or local adaptation to play a major role shaping the evolution of divergent gene regulation and gene expression in any given river system.
evidence: Based on analysis of non-parallel divergent expression in Appendix 1

claim: The transcripts showing strongest parallel expression divergence are associated with genes involved in gill ion transport and osmoregulation.
source: The transcripts showing strongest parallel expression divergence are associated with genes involved in gill ion transport and osmoregulation, a key physiological trait in marine-freshwater divergence, and in agreement with studies in other fish (Velotta et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on gene ontology enrichment analysis and citation to Velotta et al., 2017

claim: Natural selection on divergently expressed genes is shaping the evolution of the genome through strong molecular signatures of selection (elevated FST, reduced Pi) detected around the transcription start sites of parallel divergently expressed genes.
source: Through population genomic analysis, we show how natural selection on divergently expressed genes is shaping the evolution of the genome - strong molecular signatures of selection (elevated FST, reduced Pi) were detected around the transcription start sites of parallel divergently expressed genes.
evidence: Based on FST and Pi analysis around transcription start sites

claim: The predominance of cis-divergence was observed in marine-freshwater ecotypes from four independent river systems.
source: We see overwhelming evidence for the importance of cis-regulatory divergence underlying marine-freshwater gene expression divergence through analysis of allele-specific expression in F1 hybrids relative to their marine and freshwater parents. The predominance of cis-divergence was observed in marine-freshwater ecotypes from four independent river systems, in analysis of all informative transcripts genome wide, and enriched in the set of loci identified as having evolved parallel marine-freshwater divergence in expression across rivers.
evidence: Based on allele-specific expression analysis across four river systems

claim: The predominance of cis-divergence was enriched in the set of loci identified as having evolved parallel marine-freshwater divergence in expression across rivers.
source: We see overwhelming evidence for the importance of cis-regulatory divergence underlying marine-freshwater gene expression divergence through analysis of allele-specific expression in F1 hybrids relative to their marine and freshwater parents. The predominance of cis-divergence was observed in marine-freshwater ecotypes from four independent river systems, in analysis of all informative transcripts genome wide, and enriched in the set of loci identified as having evolved parallel marine-freshwater divergence in expression across rivers.
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of regulatory divergence types in parallel diverged loci

claim: Many studies have reported that cis-regulatory differences contribute strongly to divergence in gene regulation over long evolutionary divergence scales.
source: Many studies have reported that cis-regulatory differences contribute strongly to divergence in gene regulation over long evolutionary divergence scales (Coolon et al., 2014; Emerson et al., 2010; He et al., 2016; Lemmon et al., 2014; Lemos et al., 2008; Prud'homme et al., 2007; Stern and Orgogozo, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The stickleback ecotype pairs studied diverged from each other within the last 10–20 k years (approximately 10–20 k generations) following the retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheet.
source: The stickleback ecotype pairs studied here diverged from each other within the last 10–20 k years (approximately 10–20 k generations) following the retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheet, indicating that strong cis-regulatory divergence can also evolve in relatively short timescales.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about stickleback evolutionary history

claim: Strong cis-regulatory divergence can evolve in relatively short timescales (10–20 k generations).
source: The stickleback ecotype pairs studied here diverged from each other within the last 10–20 k years (approximately 10–20 k generations) following the retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheet, indicating that strong cis-regulatory divergence can also evolve in relatively short timescales.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed cis-regulatory divergence and the known timescale of divergence

claim: During maize domestication, while cis-regulatory divergence did not dominate, it did contribute to stronger magnitude regulatory changes over a relatively short evolutionary time-span.
source: For example during maize domestication, while cis-regulatory divergence did not dominate, it did contribute to stronger magnitude regulatory changes over a relatively short evolutionary time-span (Lemmon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemmon et al., 2014

claim: Within population cis-regulatory variation can be initially produced through non-adaptive processes, for example relaxed purifying selection.
source: It should also be noted that while we observe an association between nascent ecotype divergence and cis-regulatory divergence, within population cis-regulatory variation can be initially produced through non-adaptive processes, for example relaxed purifying selection (Steige et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steige et al., 2017

claim: The proportion of cis-regulatory divergence scaled positively with genomic divergence between parallel evolving stickleback ecotype-pairs.
source: While adaptation via re-use of ancient standing genetic variation is important in sticklebacks and may explain some part of the predominance of cis-regulatory changes, we also found that the extent of genomic divergence varied substantially between the parallel evolving stickleback ecotype-pairs we studied, and the proportion of cis-regulatory divergence scaled positively with this genomic divergence.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between cis-divergence and genomic divergence

claim: Much of the genetic differences that accumulate in the early stages of adaptive divergence with gene flow translate to cis-regulatory differences.
source: This suggests that much of the genetic differences that accumulate in the early stages of adaptive divergence with gene flow translate to cis-regulatory differences.
evidence: Based on inference from the positive correlation between genomic divergence and cis-regulatory divergence

claim: Mutation-accumulation experiments have shown that genetic drift, which promotes random regulatory changes, is biased toward trans-acting divergence due to a larger trans-mutational target size.
source: Mutation-accumulation experiments have shown that genetic drift, which promotes random regulatory changes, is biased toward trans-acting divergence due to a larger trans-mutational target size (Landry et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Landry et al., 2007b

claim: Most expression changes between freshwater and marine ecotypes tended to be due to divergence in cis-, which points toward a stronger contribution of selection rather than drift.
source: Since most expression changes between freshwater and marine ecotypes, however, tended to be due to divergence in cis-, this points toward a stronger contribution of selection rather than drift.
evidence: Based on inference from the predominance of cis-divergence and comparison to expectations under drift

claim: Reinforcing cis and trans-acting regulatory divergence that act in a manner to amplify one another, although rare, has an important contribution to early ecotype divergence with gene flow.
source: Our results further indicate that reinforcing cis and trans-acting regulatory divergence that act in a manner to amplify one another, although rare, has an important contribution to early ecotype divergence with gene flow.
evidence: Based on analysis of cis+trans regulatory divergence

claim: Overrepresentation in cis+trans coevolution seemed to grow with increasing genetic and expression divergence between lineages.
source: Overrepresentation in cis+trans coevolution seemed to grow with increasing genetic and expression divergence between lineages, which is notable in the context of incipient ecological speciation.
evidence: Based on observation of patterns of cis+trans divergence across populations with different levels of divergence

claim: Given enough evolutionary time, the accumulation of amplifying cis+trans regulatory divergence independently in diverging populations may lead to the evolution of genetic (Bateson-Dobzhansky-Muller) incompatibilities.
source: Given enough evolutionary time, the accumulation of amplifying cis+trans regulatory divergence independently in diverging populations may lead to the evolution of genetic (Bateson-Dobzhansky-Muller) incompatibilities.
evidence: Based on speculation about long-term consequences of cis+trans divergence

claim: Selection would favor linkage disequilibrium between coevolved cis- and trans-regulatory factors because recombination between them disrupts their combined phenotypic effects.
source: Because recombination between coevolved cis- and trans-regulatory factors disrupts their combined phenotypic effects, it is expected that selection would favor linkage disequilibrium between the coevolved regulatory factors (Verta et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on theoretical expectation and citation to Verta et al., 2016

claim: Association between increasing proportion of divergence in cis+trans regulation and genome-wide divergence suggests that selection against recombination between coevolved regulatory factors may contribute to increased genetic divergence as adaptation proceeds and thus shape the genomic landscape of incipient speciation.
source: Association between increasing proportion of divergence in cis+trans regulation and genome-wide divergence as seen here suggests that selection against recombination between coevolved regulatory factors may contribute to increased genetic divergence as adaptation proceeds and thus shape the genomic landscape of incipient speciation.
evidence: Based on inference from observed association between cis+trans divergence and genomic divergence

claim: Parallelism was identified not only in the predominance of cis- divergent gene expression across marine-freshwater ecotype pairs, but also in the quantitative extent of both cis- and trans- regulation of divergently expressed loci.
source: We not only identified parallelism across marine-freshwater ecotype pairs in the predominance of cis- divergent gene expression, but also parallelism in the quantitative extent of both cis- and trans- regulation of divergently expressed loci.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of cis- and trans-divergence across populations

claim: Strong parallelism in the quantitative extent of cis- and trans- regulation was particularly notable in parallel divergently expressed genes that are upregulated in freshwater ecotypes.
source: This strong parallelism was particularly notable in parallel divergently expressed genes that are upregulated in freshwater ecotypes, and considerably less strong and less predictable in parallel divergently expressed genes that are downregulated in freshwater.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis showing asymmetry between upregulated and downregulated genes

claim: Parallelism in the quantitative extent of cis- and trans- regulation was considerably less strong and less predictable in parallel divergently expressed genes that are downregulated in freshwater.
source: This strong parallelism was particularly notable in parallel divergently expressed genes that are upregulated in freshwater ecotypes, and considerably less strong and less predictable in parallel divergently expressed genes that are downregulated in freshwater.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis showing asymmetry between upregulated and downregulated genes

claim: The magnitude and extent of cis- and trans- upregulation of divergently expressed genes is likely to be shared among freshwater populations.
source: Similar to the underlying shared genetic basis of freshwater adaptation due to the parallel reuse of standing genetic variation, our results suggest we can not only predict that freshwater populations are likely to carry the same alleles at adaptive loci across the genome, but also that the magnitude and extent of cis- and trans- upregulation of divergently expressed genes is likely to be shared among freshwater populations.
evidence: Based on inference from observed parallelism in cis- and trans-regulation

claim: There may be fewer molecular mechanisms available to freshwater fish to 'turn on' gene expression and more diverse mechanisms to 'turn-off' gene expression.
source: It is possible that there are fewer molecular mechanisms available to freshwater fish to 'turn on' gene expression and more diverse mechanisms to 'turn-off' gene expression.
evidence: Based on speculation to explain asymmetry in parallelism between upregulated and downregulated genes

claim: The cis- and trans-regulatory effect size of genes upregulated in freshwater tended to be of larger magnitude than the cis- and trans-regulatory effects of genes downregulated in freshwater.
source: Coinciding with the stronger parallelism in genes upregulated in freshwater, we observed a tendency for the cis- and trans-regulatory effect size to be of larger magnitude than the cis- and trans-regulatory effects of genes downregulated in freshwater.
evidence: Based on analysis of effect sizes shown in Figure 5

claim: The larger effect size of genes upregulated in freshwater enables selection to be more efficient and contributes to the observed stronger parallelism.
source: It is plausible that this larger effect size enables selection to be more efficient and contributes to the observed stronger parallelism.
evidence: Based on speculation about the relationship between effect size and parallelism

claim: The marine ecotype is thought to be the ancestral state in threespine sticklebacks and has been evolving in a comparatively stable marine environment for millions of years.
source: Further, the marine ecotype is thought to be the ancestral state in threespine sticklebacks and has been evolving in a comparatively stable marine environment for millions of years.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about stickleback evolutionary history

claim: Freshwater populations have a comparatively smaller effective population size with reduced access to pre-existing adaptive standing genetic variation, and have been subject to more recent and potentially stronger selection pressures than their marine ecotype counterparts.
source: Under this evolutionary context, freshwater populations have a comparatively smaller effective population size with reduced access to pre-existing adaptive standing genetic variation, and have been subject to more recent and potentially stronger selection pressures than their marine ecotype counterparts.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about stickleback population history and ecology

claim: Marine ecotypes have more opportunity to evolve via soft sweeps on standing genetic variation.
source: Thus, marine ecotypes have more opportunity to evolve via soft sweeps on standing genetic variation.
evidence: Based on inference from population size and evolutionary history

claim: The evolutionary context of sticklebacks is likely to have influenced which molecular mechanisms of gene expression regulation are visible and efficiently respond to selection, resulting in relatively few paths to evolve adaptive upregulation of gene expression in freshwater populations compared to marine.
source: Combined this evolutionary context is likely to have influenced which molecular mechanisms of gene expression regulation are visible, and efficiently respond to selection, resulting in relatively few paths to evolve adaptive upregulation of gene expression in freshwater populations compared to marine.
evidence: Based on speculation about how evolutionary context influences regulatory evolution

claim: A recent study by Hart et al. (2018) reported a predominance of, and parallelism in, the trans-regulatory control of marine-freshwater divergent gene expression in the pharyngeal tooth plate.
source: We note that our results contrast with a recent study by Hart et al. (2018) who reported a predominance of, and parallelism in, the trans-regulatory control of marine-freshwater divergent gene expression in the pharyngeal tooth plate.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hart et al., 2018

claim: Differences in the multifunctional (pleiotropic) functional roles of the gill and its likely complex genetic architecture compared to dental tissue with a less pleiotropic functional role and more simple genetic architecture might explain the contrast with Hart et al. (2018).
source: One possible biological explanation for this might be differences in the multifunctional (pleiotropic) functional roles of the gill and its likely complex genetic architecture compared to dental tissue with a less pleiotropic functional role and more simple genetic architecture involving a few large effect loci upstream of other factors (Cleves et al., 2014) that cause a dominant trans-regulatory signal in the allele-specific expression assay.
evidence: Based on speculation about tissue-specific differences and citation to Cleves et al., 2014

claim: Parallel evolving divergence may converge on cis-regulatory changes driven in part by a higher level of additivity and lower level of epistasis of cis-regulatory factors.
source: Our results indicate that parallel evolving divergence may converge on cis-regulatory changes driven in part by a higher level of additivity and lower level of epistasis of cis-regulatory factors.
evidence: Based on analysis of additivity and epistasis of different regulatory classes

claim: The fixation of beneficial recessive alleles are hindered due to its phenotype being hidden from selection (Haldane's sieve).
source: Known as the effect of 'Haldane's sieve', the fixation of beneficial recessive alleles are hindered due to its phenotype being hidden from selection (Haldane, 1927).
evidence: Based on established theory and citation to Haldane, 1927

claim: When alternative alleles are favored in their respective environments, additive alleles have the highest likelihood of becoming fixed in both populations as both alleles can rise quickly to a high frequency.
source: When alternative alleles are favored in their respective environments, as seem to be the case in sticklebacks, additive alleles have the highest likelihood of becoming fixed in both populations as both alleles can rise quickly to a high frequency.
evidence: Based on theoretical expectation about selection on additive alleles

claim: Cis-regulatory variation tended to have a lower level of epistasis within populations compared to other types of regulatory effects.
source: Cis-regulatory variation also tended to have a lower level of epistasis within populations compared to other types of regulatory effects.
evidence: Based on analysis of regulatory divergence sharing between siblings

claim: Epistatic regulatory alleles tend to have different phenotypic effects depending on the genetic background, therefore inducing unpredictable fluctuation in expression levels.
source: Epistatic regulatory alleles tend to have different phenotypic effects depending on the genetic background, therefore inducing unpredictable fluctuation in expression levels.
evidence: Based on established understanding of epistasis

claim: Parallel evolution of gene expression seems to favor non-epistatic regulatory alleles that have similar effects on expression levels independently of the genetic background.
source: Hence, parallel evolution of gene expression seems to favor non-epistatic regulatory alleles that have similar effects on expression levels independently of the genetic background.
evidence: Based on inference from observed lower epistasis of cis-regulatory divergence

claim: Adaptation-with-gene-flow is predicted to promote reduced expression plasticity, especially in cases where selection is strong.
source: In addition to promoting divergence in expression levels that is independent of genetic backgrounds, adaptation-with-gene-flow is predicted to promote reduced expression plasticity, especially in cases where selection is strong (Stern and Orgogozo, 2009).
evidence: Based on theoretical prediction and citation to Stern and Orgogozo, 2009

claim: Divergence in cis-regulation may play a particularly important role in the evolution of reduced plasticity.
source: Toward this end, our results indicate that divergence in cis-regulation may play a particularly important role in the evolution of reduced plasticity.
evidence: Based on inference from salinity experiment results

claim: Plasticity is known to be involved in the divergent adaptation of marine and freshwater sticklebacks.
source: Since plasticity is known to be involved in the divergent adaptation of marine and freshwater sticklebacks we investigated the sensitivity of gene expression and its cis- and trans-regulation to environmental salinity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about plasticity in sticklebacks

claim: Genetic assimilation involves the heritable encoding and loss of plasticity of a once plastic trait.
source: Genetic assimilation involves the heritable encoding and loss of plasticity of a once plastic trait (Waddington, 1942).
evidence: Based on established concept and citation to Waddington, 1942

claim: Previous studies have found evidence for genetic assimilation in gill gene expression evolution between stickleback ecotypes.
source: Previous studies have found evidence for genetic assimilation in gill gene expression evolution between stickleback ecotypes (McCairns and Bernatchez, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCairns and Bernatchez, 2010

claim: While there was a strong component of plasticity in gene expression among siblings raised in different salinities, the cis-regulation of this gene expression was stable and insensitive to differences in the environmental conditions.
source: While we found a strong component of plasticity in gene expression among siblings raised in different salinities, the cis-regulation of this gene expression was stable and insensitive to differences in the environmental conditions.
evidence: Based on analysis of expression and allele-specific expression across salinities

claim: The observed plasticity in expression is likely mediated via trans-regulation.
source: From this we infer that the observed plasticity in expression is likely mediated via trans-regulation, and hypothesize that the stable divergence in cis-regulation component may serve as a mechanism for genetic assimilation.
evidence: Based on inference from the stability of cis-regulation across salinities

claim: The stable divergence in cis-regulation component may serve as a mechanism for genetic assimilation.
source: From this we infer that the observed plasticity in expression is likely mediated via trans-regulation, and hypothesize that the stable divergence in cis-regulation component may serve as a mechanism for genetic assimilation.
evidence: Based on hypothesis derived from salinity experiment results

claim: The loci with parallel expression divergence that are predominantly regulated by cis-acting changes are dispersed throughout the genome but proximal to previously identified adaptive loci.
source: The loci with parallel expression divergence that are predominantly regulated by cis-acting changes are dispersed throughout the genome but proximal to previously identified adaptive loci.
evidence: Based on genomic distribution and proximity analysis

claim: Signatures of selection around transcription start sites of parallel diverged loci are likely to be a result of natural selection acting on cis-regulatory elements.
source: We observed signatures of selection around their transcription start sites likely to be a result of natural selection acting on cis-regulatory elements.
evidence: Based on inference from FST and Pi patterns around transcription start sites

claim: Cis-regulatory divergence acts in an additive manner and is robust to both different environmental contexts, and potential epistasis caused by differences in genetic background.
source: We show that cis-regulatory divergence acts in an additive manner and is robust to both different environmental contexts, and potential epistasis caused by differences in genetic background.
evidence: Based on analysis of additivity, epistasis, and salinity response

claim: Cis-regulation of divergently expressed loci upregulated in freshwater shows parallelism and large magnitude effect sizes across marine-freshwater ecotype pairs from independent river systems.
source: Comparing across marine-freshwater ecotype pairs from independent river systems, we observed parallelism and large magnitude effect sizes for cis-regulation of divergently expressed loci upregulated in freshwater.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis and effect size analysis across populations

claim: The features of cis-divergence (additivity, robustness, parallelism, large effect sizes) make it a well-poised target for natural selection and may explain parallelism in the predominance and quantitative extent of cis-divergence in the early stages intraspecific adaptive divergence.
source: These features make cis-divergence a well-poised target for natural selection and may explain parallelism in the predominance and quantitative extent of cis-divergence in the early stages intraspecific adaptive divergence.
evidence: Based on inference from observed properties of cis-divergence

claim: Natural selection on adaptive cis-divergence is a likely contributor to the dispersed genomic landscape of adaptation in sticklebacks.
source: Combined our study highlights how natural selection on adaptive cis-divergence is a likely contributor to the dispersed genomic landscape of adaptation in sticklebacks.
evidence: Based on inference from the dispersed genomic distribution of parallel diverged loci and their cis-regulatory control

claim: Cis-acting (allele-specific) regulation consistently predominates gene expression divergence in threespine stickleback gill tissue from four independent marine-freshwater ecotype pairs.
source: Using RNAseq of threespine stickleback fish gill tissue from four independent marine-freshwater ecotype pairs and their F1 hybrids, we show that cis-acting (allele-specific) regulation consistently predominates gene expression divergence.
evidence: Based on allele-specific expression analysis across four ecotype pairs

claim: Genes showing parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence are found near to adaptive genomic regions.
source: Genes showing parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence are found near to adaptive genomic regions, show signatures of natural selection around their transcription start sites and are enriched for cis-regulatory control.
evidence: Based on proximity analysis to adaptive loci

claim: Genes showing parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence show signatures of natural selection around their transcription start sites.
source: Genes showing parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence are found near to adaptive genomic regions, show signatures of natural selection around their transcription start sites and are enriched for cis-regulatory control.
evidence: Based on FST and Pi analysis around transcription start sites

claim: Genes showing parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence are enriched for cis-regulatory control.
source: Genes showing parallel marine-freshwater expression divergence are found near to adaptive genomic regions, show signatures of natural selection around their transcription start sites and are enriched for cis-regulatory control.
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of regulatory divergence types

claim: For genes with parallel increased expression among freshwater fish, the quantitative degree of cis- and trans-regulation is highly correlated across populations.
source: For genes with parallel increased expression among freshwater fish, the quantitative degree of cis- and trans-regulation is also highly correlated across populations, suggesting a shared genetic basis.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of cis- and trans-divergence across populations

claim: The high correlation in cis- and trans-regulation across populations for genes with parallel increased expression among freshwater fish suggests a shared genetic basis.
source: For genes with parallel increased expression among freshwater fish, the quantitative degree of cis- and trans-regulation is also highly correlated across populations, suggesting a shared genetic basis.
evidence: Based on inference from observed correlation

claim: Compared to other forms of regulation, cis-regulation tends to show greater additivity and stability across different genetic and environmental contexts.
source: Compared to other forms of regulation, cis-regulation tends to show greater additivity and stability across different genetic and environmental contexts, making it a fertile substrate for the early stages of adaptive evolution.
evidence: Based on analysis of additivity, epistasis, and salinity response

claim: The greater additivity and stability of cis-regulation across different genetic and environmental contexts makes it a fertile substrate for the early stages of adaptive evolution.
source: Compared to other forms of regulation, cis-regulation tends to show greater additivity and stability across different genetic and environmental contexts, making it a fertile substrate for the early stages of adaptive evolution.
evidence: Based on inference from observed properties of cis-regulation
